title: Peter Stone - Outplaying Elite Table Tennis Players with an Autonomous Robot

segments.text: PETER STONE: Thanks for the introduction.
Thanks all for being here.
So as I said, I am coming from UT Austin and Tony AI.
I'm going to talk mainly about a recent result from Sony
AI on the first robot that can beat a professional athlete
at their own sport.
So I'll talk about that mainly.
But first, I'll tell you, I am coming from UT Austin.
In two weeks, I'm going to be the head of a new school
of computing there that brings together
three different departments.
I was the founding director of Texas Robotics.
We're going to be hosting the conference on robot
learning this fall in November.
I hope to see many of you there.
And if you come, you'll get a chance
to see our beautiful new robotics facility.
Anna Hiss Gym, it used to be the women's gymnasium when there
was such a thing as women's gymnasium,
but now it's filled with robots.
We also have a machine learning laboratory.
I'm deeply involved in ethical AI initiative
called Good Systems.
And I'm really proud of the AI education
that we've been doing there, including
a publicly available, anybody-can-use full course
on AI literacy, essentials of AI for life and society.
That's for non-majors or anybody, really.
And also, an online masters for $10,000.
My research is fairly broad, but the question
that unites all the things I've done over the years
is this one, to what degree can autonomous,
intelligent agents learn in the presence of teammates
and/or adversaries in real-time dynamic domains?
So my group publishes in the subareas of AI shown here,
especially multiagent systems, robotics,
and reinforcement learning.
And some of the applications domains
that I've used over the years have
been things like robot soccer.
So here's a video from many years ago.
Our team was the one with their hands
behind their-- the arm behind their back.
We ended up winning this competition with the Nao robots,
where you have to remember these robots are fully autonomous.
The goal of RoboCup is by the year 2050,
to have a team of humanoid robots
that can beat the best World Cup team on a real soccer field.
We're not quite there yet.
But things have advanced since that video.
Just a month ago, our team is shown in blue here.
These are bigger and faster humanoid robots.
These are made by a company called Booster.
It's a beautiful robot.
But then we did all the programming.
And it's a learned skill here of walking and kicking, using
reinforcement learning.
And gotten to the point where we can now do human--
it makes sense to put humans and robots on the same field.
So here's a clip where I take the ball
and leave the ball for the robot.
And see what happens.
The robot's able to turn and score a goal, so.
I also work on general purpose service robots.
So things like this.
At RoboCup, there's also a competition
called RoboCup@Home, where a robot has to do things
like putting away groceries, setting the table,
interacting with visitors.
And so this is a great domain for general purpose robots.
And then prior to this, the table tennis
result that I'm about to talk to you about, my team at Sony AI
had a paper on the cover of Nature
about four years ago, where we were the first AI agent
to be able to beat the very best humans at a real-time control
task, in this case Gran Turismo.
So in this video, the green cars are
trained with end-to-end reinforcement learning.
The white ones are driven by some of the best drivers
in the world at Gran Turismo.
We outperformed them.
And that was featured in Nature.
And now, I also work on also navigation,
not just in road settings, but in more social settings.
This is joint work with Joydeep Biswas, where
we have robots navigating through the hike and bike trails
through Austin, having to navigate social situations.
But the title of my talk and the main thing
I'm going to tell you about is a result called ACE with my team
at Sony AI.
Oh, one other thing I wanted to tell you about because we just
publicized it a couple days ago is a data set that we're
collecting called Oopsie Data, which is about robot failures.
So most data sets are about robots doing successful things.
This is a community-sourced effort
to try to gather failure data from robots.
And we hope that many of you will contribute to this.
So look it up.
There's a way to contribute and annotate what the failures were.
Postdoc in my lab, Claas Voelcker, has been leading that.
But the main topic of this talk is the a group--
trying to create a table tennis player
with this group at Sony AI.
Of course, it's not just my work.
It's a large team.
It was led by Peter Dürr.
He's really deserves the lion's share of the credit here.
But a huge team effort.
It was featured on the cover of Nature in April 23.
So just three months ago or so.
And so you can read all about it there and get all the details.
But the motivation here is that games
have been a benchmark for AI for many years
in turn-taking settings like chess and go
and poker and then some more real-time settings.
As I said, GT Sophy was the first real-time control
task where humans did better.
The first real-world outperforming the best humans
was drone racing.
That was Davide Scaramuzza's lab that was also featured
on, I think, a cover of Nature.
But that was not in a competitive head-to-head
setting.
Meanwhile, table tennis is one-on-one, adversarial,
and has been used as a motivator for robotics research for many
years, going back to the mid 1980s.
This is a video from Google.
And Vincent, who's the next speaker,
played a role in this one, where a robot was playing very well
in a cooperative setting.
But there had been no example of a competitive robot that's
able to beat expert-level players using Olympic rules.
And so in this video I'm going to show you,
our robot on the right is playing
against a woman who has twice won an Olympic silver medal.
She was once ranked fifth in the world.
I think at the time we played her,
she was ranked 11th in the world, something like that.
And the robot is playing according
to professional regulations.
So the player's area is the same.
The robot has to serve the ball, which has not always
been the case in systems.
So it has a cup where it can toss the ball up and serve it.
And so I'm not going to be able to go through all the details
here.
But the general system setup is that there's-- obviously,
it's not a humanoid robot.
And so the form factor is that we actually
built the robot custom made and engineered
it to be as light as possible.
It has to be able to move 20 meters--
hit the ball 20 meters per second every 8/10 of a second.
That's to get to professional-level play.
The cameras are all around the system.
There's nine that are positioned to get
xyz coordinates of the ball and then three that are event-based
gaze control cameras that can track
the spin of the ball, which I'll show you in a minute.
And this is an overhead view, where you see the player
area and the robot workspace.
The only concession that we make to this being a robot
is that we don't allow the player
to cross the net for safety reasons.
But otherwise, it's effectively regulation Olympic rules.
The robot learns to play in simulation.
So the three main contributions in the Nature article
are the perception system, the reinforcement learning
for control, and then the hardware of the robot itself.
The main control problem for us was figuring out
as the ball is coming in, how do you
move the arm of the robot to be able to hit the ball, given
a particular target and spin that you want to realize?
And we call that a skill as opposed to tactics, which
would be where do you-- choosing where
do you want to hit the ball or strategy, which would be longer
term, what do I want to do from point to point or even game
to game?
So most of our RRL is at this low-level skill level.
Much of it in simulation.
But where the data is it's a physics-informed simulator--
sorry, I keep jumping-- the physics-informed simulator,
where there's data from the real world that builds the noise
model, the ball distribution model, and the physics model.
And then there's an actor critic, where it's asymmetric.
There's a true state given to the critic and a noisy state
given to the actor.
And then the actor is what runs in the real world.
I won't go into the-- one of the big technical things
we needed to do was come up with an action space
that the robot could deal with because we have-- it's
a 6 degree of freedom arm on 2 degrees of freedom for the base.
And so there's a very counterintuitive set
of space points that the end effector could get to.
And we find a way to map that to a hypercube, such
that any point in that hypercube is a feasible.
So we call this feasible action for optimal control.
And then there's a model predictive controller
that controls the end effector to try
to get the target that is chosen by the reinforcement learning
agent.
So this video will show you how the robot can react quickly.
You're going to slow it down and see as it hits the net,
the robot was trying to hit a forehand.
But then after the ball hits the net,
it adjusts and then swings its arm back the other way
and is able to still hit the ball back.
So here's it, again, in real time.
Oops.
In real time.
You'll see how quickly the robot responds.
And we have several examples on the blog and on our website,
showing examples of the robot responding to these net balls
in real time.
I said there's the event-based camera that's tracking the spin.
There's no artificial marker on the ball.
So it's just using the logo that's there.
So here's what that event-based camera
sees as the robot is spinning.
So the mirror shown here on the left
is tracking where the ball is in xyz coordinates.
And then in real time, we're able to determine
the speed and the spin of the ball, which is then
given as input to the RL agent.
This is a robot video where you have to slow it down
to be able to watch it.
Most robot videos, you see them sped up a lot.
Here's a nice video from the viewpoint of the robot.
It's a camera mounted on the arm.
And again, slowed down.
So you can see it's tracking the spin and speed of the ball
and then deciding how it should hit it.
I said the other contribution here was the robot itself.
It's a custom-built robot where we use an optimization process
to take away all of the mass of the robot that isn't needed
for structural stability and reduced it
5 kilograms from the original design
so that we could achieve the high speeds at high frequency,
where there's six revolute joints and two joints on the xy
plane on the base.
And then there's also a serve library
that's done using an evolutionary process,
where we have to-- where we get a diversity of serves.
So it's not predictable to the player.
And then the robot will pick one of them to execute.
But it's trying to find some that have backspin, topspin,
different locations.
And all of those are trained to be able to start off the point
before it moves to the standard RL controller
for the rest of the rally.
Just in terms of results, the Nature article
has results up until December 2025, where we were beating--
where we were losing sometimes, but beating
some university-level players.
The ones shown in red are losses.
The ones in green, we won at least one game against them.
If there's a T in the top, that means they're
a professional-level player.
And then recently, just a month or so ago,
we released a blog with all the results from this past spring,
where we did meet a woman who was ranked fifth in the world
at one point, a man who was ranked 99th in the world at one
point.
So really beating professional-level players.
And then this is just showing some
of the data of how fast the ball is
being able to hit both back in April 2025 and 2026.
We're hitting the ball slightly faster than professional humans,
not quite putting enough as much spin as professional humans.
And this is showing just another match against the--
he was, I think, ranked 99th in the world.
Male professionals hit the ball harder
than the female professionals.
But we're able to beat him as well,
even at really fast speeds.
And so all of these videos or available online.
And I'll just-- in summary, in this video,
which will be the last one I show, is a warm-up video.
It's the first time this woman was-- this professional woman
was playing with the robot.
And so it's not trying to beat her.
It's this warm-up phase.
But you'll see at the end of the point
that she's really having fun, is really impressed and enjoying
herself.
But the summary here is that for the first time,
we've shown that AI agents can reach expert-level performance
in tasks that require fast, real-time decision-making
in physical space.
There's still many open questions.
Can the robot be the world champion?
We don't know.
Can expert table tennis players use these robots
to improve their game?
We actually do have some examples
already of professionals getting ideas of shots
that they wouldn't have otherwise tried.
And could we do this with a humanoid?
I think we're still very far from that.
But there's, like I said, lots more information on this online.
And there'll also be a talk on the main stage at 3:10,
I believe, Michael Spranger is the president of Sony AI.
He has a 10-minute talk.
He'll talk a little bit about this
and some of the other projects at Sony AI, including GT--
more about GT Sophy, the high-speed racing agent.
So with that, thank you for your attention.
I'll be around if there's any questions afterwards.
[APPLAUSE]
